summary: A brief correction of several errors in RFC 567's bandwidth calculation. It notes, for example, that not all packets are 1000 bits long, and gives the actual sizes of RFNM messages and of Host-Host protocol messages.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 568 corrects the packet-size calculations in RFC 567's discussion of remote echoing. It argues that delays, rather than total network bandwidth, are the main cause of poor echo response.

questions: how big is an arpanet rfnm
subtitle: A correction to packet-size estimates in a discussion of remote echoing and network bandwidth.

tldr.problem: RFC 567's estimate of bandwidth used by remote character echo relied on packet-size assumptions that McQuillan says are incorrect.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 568 gives sizes for RFNMs and Host-Host messages and argues that the resulting load is far below the earlier estimate.
tldr.outcome: The author argues that slow echo response is mainly a delay problem, while agreeing that TELNET changes can reduce traffic and host processing.

today: The unit records RFC 568's status as Unknown and says it updates RFC 567. It is a correction to RFC 567's bandwidth calculations for remote echoing.

sections.title: Correcting the Packet Assumptions
sections.content:
McQuillan says RFC 567 makes several fundamental errors, beginning with the assumption that all packets are 1000 bits long. The RFC states that packet sizes vary and gives separate sizes for return-to-host messages and Host-Host protocol messages.

It gives an RFNM size of 152 bits and a single-character or allocate Host-Host message size of 216 bits. The author's calculation totals 736 bits in each direction, rather than 4000 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier estimate treated every packet as the same size. This correction uses the sizes of the message types involved in remote echoing.

sections.title: Traffic Rate and Buffering
sections.content:
From the revised message sizes, McQuillan estimates that the network can support over 200 single-character messages per second, not 37.5. He notes that this pattern is unlikely and that the IMP subnetwork can support it more readily than most hosts.

If remote-echo demand exceeded network capacity, TIPs and hosts could buffer two characters per message, which the RFC says would double effective bandwidth. It also says that packing more characters into a message can increase effective bandwidth nearly proportionally, with responses slowing as load rises.
sections.plainLanguage: The corrected sizes allow many more single-character messages than the earlier estimate. Grouping characters into a message can also reduce the effect of message overhead.

sections.title: Why Echoing Can Still Be Slow
sections.content:
The RFC argues that poor echo response is mainly a delay problem, not a bandwidth problem. The IMP software was designed to give interactive traffic low delay and bulk transfers high throughput; short messages have high overhead in bits and processor wake-ups.

As an extreme illustration, the author says echoing over a megabit-per-second satellite link could lag a second or more even without bandwidth limits. He agrees that TELNET changes may improve performance by reducing network traffic and host processing, especially on long-delay paths such as satellite links.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can have plenty of capacity and still feel slow if each response takes a long time to travel. The author supports TELNET changes that reduce the work and traffic involved.

references.text: Deutsch, L. P., Cross-Country Network Bandwidth, RFC 567.
